idiom_name: return-code checks with explicit fallback values behind a degradation flag
implementation_notes: C has no exceptions and no standard-library fallback: every call returns a status (or sets errno) that the caller must test, and the substitute is an ordinary value written into an out-parameter. The classic structure is hand-rolled from a status convention plus a small state flag (an int/atomic, or a per-dependency function pointer) that the response builder consults; errno is only meaningful immediately after a failed call, so capture it there. Keep the fallback path resource-clean: the same free()/close() obligations apply when the primary call fails halfway through.
pitfalls: errno is only valid until the next library call (and is thread-local on POSIX): copy it immediately and never test it after the fallback ran.
A partially filled output struct with no separate status is indistinguishable from success - always return the status out of band.
The degraded path must release everything the failed attempt acquired (buffers, descriptors, locks); leak-free fallbacks are the part that is usually wrong.
